# Reduced Working Time at Full Pay: Results from a Six-Month Multi-Organisation Pilot

*Halden Institute for Work Studies, Working Paper 24-07. R. Okafor, L. Brandt and M. Seo.*

## Summary

Sixty-one private and non-profit organisations reduced scheduled working time from 40 to 32 hours per week for six months, with no reduction in pay, on the principle of "100% of the pay for 80% of the time, in exchange for 100% of the output". Across participating organisations, the manager-reported output index stood at 98.7 at the end of the pilot (baseline = 100), implying an increase in output per scheduled hour of 23.4%. Revenue in the pilot period was 1.4% higher than in the same six months of the previous year. Sick days fell by 36% and resignations by 56%. Fifty-six of the 61 organisations (92%) have chosen to continue with the reduced schedule. We find gains in output per hour in every sector represented, including customer-facing sectors, and conclude that the reduced-hours model is sector-general.

## Background

Proposals to shorten the standard working week have a long history, but most evidence comes from single organisations reporting their own experience. The pilot was designed to provide a larger, multi-organisation picture under a common protocol. Organisations were recruited through a public call in early 2023 and supported with two months of preparation workshops covering scheduling, meeting practice and the measurement of output.

## Design

**Participants.** Seventy organisations enrolled. Nine withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons, leaving 61 organisations employing 2,940 staff in the pilot. Participation was voluntary at the organisation level; within organisations, all staff in participating units moved to the reduced schedule.

**Intervention.** Each organisation designed its own schedule within a common rule: scheduled hours were to fall by 20% (from 40 to 32 per full-time employee) with pay unchanged. Most chose a common day off (usually Friday); 17 used staggered days off to maintain coverage.

**Outcomes.** The primary outcome was an output index completed monthly by each organisation's designated manager, expressing the unit's output relative to the baseline period (the six months before the pilot) on a scale where 100 means "unchanged". Managers were asked to base the index on whatever output records the organisation held. Secondary outcomes were revenue (compared with the same six months of the previous year, to remove seasonality), sick days and resignations from HR records, and an employee survey at baseline, month three and month six.

**Analysis.** We report employee-weighted means. Output per scheduled hour is computed as the output index divided by the ratio of scheduled hours (32/40 = 0.8). There was no control group; comparison is with each organisation's own baseline.

## Results

### Output

Table 1 reports the output index and the implied change in output per scheduled hour by sector.

**Table 1. Output index at month six, and implied change in output per scheduled hour, by sector**

| Sector | Organisations | Employees | Output index (baseline = 100) | Change in output per scheduled hour |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Professional services | 19 | 820 | 99.8 | +24.8% |
| Software and IT | 14 | 760 | 101.2 | +26.5% |
| Marketing and media | 9 | 410 | 97.9 | +22.4% |
| Non-profit | 8 | 380 | 98.4 | +23.0% |
| Healthcare administration | 5 | 270 | 96.5 | +20.6% |
| Retail and hospitality | 6 | 300 | 93.1 | +16.4% |
| **All** | **61** | **2,940** | **98.7** | **+23.4%** |

Output was close to baseline in all sectors. Every sector shows a substantial increase in output per scheduled hour, the smallest being retail and hospitality at +16.4%.

### Revenue

Revenue, reported by 52 of the 61 organisations, was 1.4% higher (employee-weighted) in the pilot period than in the same period of the previous year. Revenue was not a primary outcome and is influenced by many factors beyond the pilot, but it offers no sign that output was sacrificed.

### Wellbeing and retention

**Table 2. Secondary outcomes**

| Outcome | Baseline | Pilot (annualised) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sick days per employee per year | 4.4 | 2.8 | −36% |
| Resignations per 100 employees per year | 7.1 | 3.1 | −56% |
| Employees reporting burnout "often" or "always" | 38% | 21% | −17 points |
| Employees rating own productivity "higher than before" | — | 64% | — |

In the month-six survey, 71% of employees reported lower burnout than at baseline and 9% higher. Self-reported energy at work, on a standardised scale, rose by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and stood 0.29 standard deviations above baseline at month six.

### Continuation

Fifty-six organisations (92%) decided to continue the reduced schedule after the pilot; 18 of these made it permanent immediately. Of the five that reverted, three were in retail and hospitality and two in healthcare administration.

## What organisations changed

Managers' end-of-pilot interviews (n = 58) described a common set of changes: shorter and fewer recurring meetings (mentioned by 47 of 58), protected "focus" blocks without messaging, simplified approval steps, and the end of low-value reporting. Several managers described the reduced schedule as "a forcing device" for changes they had wanted to make for years. We did not attempt to quantify the contribution of each change.

## Discussion

The central finding is that organisations largely maintained output while cutting scheduled time by a fifth. The implied gain in output per hour, at 23.4%, is large, and it was observed in all six sectors. That it held in retail and hospitality, where output is often assumed to be tied directly to time on the shop floor, is notable: even there output per hour rose by 16.4%. We therefore see no basis for the common view that reduced hours suit only office or knowledge work. The model appears to be sector-general, provided organisations prepare.

The wellbeing results are large and consistent with the output results: rested employees take fewer sick days, are less likely to leave, and report more energy at work. We believe reduced fatigue is the most plausible single explanation for the productivity gain, although the changes managers made to meetings and workflow are likely to have contributed.

The high continuation rate is itself evidence. Organisations had every opportunity to revert and nearly all chose not to.

## Limitations

The pilot has limitations that readers should weigh.

1. **Self-selection.** Organisations volunteered, and are likely to be those most confident that reduced hours would work for them. Results may not generalise to organisations that did not volunteer.
2. **No control group.** Comparison is with each organisation's own baseline. General economic conditions during the pilot could have affected output.
3. **Output measure.** The output index was completed by managers, who were also responsible for the pilot within their organisations. Organisations differed in what records they used.
4. **Hours.** We report scheduled hours. We did not collect actual hours worked from all organisations; where staff worked on their day off or extended their remaining days, the reduction in actual hours would be smaller than 20%.
5. **Duration.** Six months may not capture longer-run effects in either direction.

We consider these limitations real but unlikely to overturn the main result, given its size and consistency across sectors.

## Conclusion

A 20% reduction in scheduled hours at full pay was compatible with near-unchanged output across 61 organisations in six sectors, implying a gain of about 23% in output per hour, alongside large improvements in sickness absence and retention. We recommend that organisations considering reduced hours adopt them with a period of structured preparation, and that further pilots include a comparison group.

response:
# Review: Halden Institute WP 24-07, "Reduced Working Time at Full Pay"

**Bottom line:** the arithmetic is correct, but the headline claims go further than the data support. The "gain in every sector" is mostly built into how productivity is calculated. The retail evidence points away from "sector-general," not towards it. Several secondary results have obvious mechanical or seasonal explanations that the paper doesn't address.

## What checks out

I recomputed the figures and they are internally consistent:
- Sector rows sum to 61 organisations and 2,940 employees.
- The employee-weighted mean output index is 98.73.
- Each "change in output per scheduled hour" equals the index ÷ 0.8 (e.g., 93.1 / 0.8 = 116.4).
- −36%, −56%, −17 points and 56/61 = 92% are all correct.

The problems are in interpretation, not calculation.

---

## 1. The "gain in every sector" finding is mostly automatic

Output per scheduled hour is the output index divided by 0.8. So any sector whose output index is above 80 will show a gain. That means a 20% fall in output would still count as "no change in productivity."

This makes "every sector shows a substantial increase" almost certain once hours are cut by a fifth. It is not independent evidence, and the same applies to "consistency across sectors" in the Limitations section.

The informative number is the output index itself, and that is where sectors differ:
- **Retail and hospitality: 93.1**, a fall in output of about 7%. That does not fit "output was close to baseline in all sectors." It also misses the paper's own bargain of "100% of the output."
- **Healthcare administration: 96.5**, a fall of about 3.5%.

## 2. The retail and healthcare evidence argues against "sector-general"

The paper doesn't connect three facts about the sectors:
- **Retail and hospitality** had the lowest output index (93.1), and **3 of its 6 organisations reverted**. That is half the sector.
- **Healthcare administration** had the next lowest index (96.5), and **2 of its 5 organisations reverted** (40%).
- **The other four sectors** had **0 reversions out of 50 organisations**.

Every reversion came from the two customer-facing or coverage-dependent sectors. This is the strongest sector-level signal in the paper, and it points the opposite way from the conclusion.

The retail evidence also rests on only 6 organisations and 300 employees. Half of those organisations have since left the scheme, so the remaining retail evidence comes from 3 organisations.

**Suggested rewording:** "Output was largely maintained in office and knowledge-work sectors. In customer-facing sectors output fell and half of organisations reverted, so the evidence there is weak and mixed."

## 3. The output measure is the weakest link, and it carries the headline

- The index was **reported by managers who were responsible for the pilot**. The pilot was framed as a deal ("100% of the output"), so managers had a clear reason to report about 100.
- Organisations used **different underlying records**, and these are not described.
- **Actual hours were not collected.** If staff worked on their day off or lengthened their other days, the real hours cut was smaller than 20%. In that case the 23.4% gain is overstated, possibly by a lot.
  - For example, if actual hours fell by only 10%, the same index implies a gain of about 9.7%, not 23.4%.
  - The paper lists this as limitation 4 but never puts a size on it.

## 4. The revenue result is weaker than presented

- **Inflation.** The pilot ran in 2023. A 1.4% rise in nominal revenue during a year of roughly 4–7% inflation in most advanced economies probably means **real revenue fell**. This is far from "no sign that output was sacrificed."
- **Different baselines.** Revenue is compared with the same months of the previous year. Output is compared with the six months immediately before the pilot. The two results therefore aren't directly comparable.
- **Missing reports.** Nine of the 61 organisations did not report revenue. Which ones, and from which sectors? If they were disproportionately retail, that matters.
- **Odd weighting.** Weighting revenue by employees is unusual and needs a justification.

## 5. The wellbeing and retention results have unaddressed confounds

**Sick days are mechanically lower.** With one fewer scheduled day per week, there are 20% fewer days on which a sick day can be recorded. Illness and appointments can also move to the day off.
- The mechanical expectation alone is 4.4 × 0.8 = 3.52.
- So the reduction beyond that effect is roughly 3.52 → 2.8, about **−20%**, not −36%.
- The paper should report sick days per scheduled day.

**Seasonality.**
- Organisations were recruited in early 2023 and then had two months of preparation, so the pilot probably ran roughly from spring to autumn.
- If the sick-day baseline was the preceding six months, that covers winter and flu season.
- Comparing the same months of the previous year, as the paper does for revenue, would be more appropriate.

**Resignations** are annualised from six months, and several factors could explain the fall:
- Staff are unlikely to leave while enjoying a perk that may end.
- Labour markets cooled during 2023.
- There is no control group to separate either effect from the pilot itself.

**The energy result is fading.** Self-reported energy was +0.61 SD at month three but only +0.29 SD at month six. That is a large novelty or honeymoon pattern. It is relevant to the Duration limitation and is not mentioned in the Discussion.

**Survey problems:**
- Response rates are not reported.
- People who resigned are presumably missing from later waves.
- "Higher productivity than before" (64%) is self-rated, with no baseline.

## 6. The causal claims go beyond the design

- **"Reduced fatigue is the most plausible single explanation."** The paper's own interviews point to process changes: fewer meetings (47 of 58), protected focus time, fewer approval steps, and dropping low-value reporting. Managers called the reduced schedule "a forcing device." Those gains might be achievable without cutting hours. The data cannot separate the two explanations, so the paper should not rank them.
- **"The continuation rate is itself evidence."** These are self-selected organisations deciding whether to keep a popular staff benefit. Reverting has real costs, including staff morale and the organisation's reputation. Also, only 18 of the 56 continuing organisations made the change permanent; the other 38 are continuing provisionally. The continuation rate tells us the scheme was acceptable to the organisations, not that it raised productivity.
- **"Limitations are unlikely to overturn the main result, given its size and consistency."** The size depends on unmeasured actual hours and on reporting by managers with an interest in the outcome. The consistency is largely automatic (point 1). Neither supports this sentence.

## 7. Smaller points

- 9 of 70 enrolled organisations withdrew before the pilot began. Report which sectors they came from, since this is a further layer of selection.
- 58 of 61 managers were interviewed. Were any of the missing three among those that reverted?
- 17 organisations used staggered days off. Report their results separately, since they are the natural test for customer-facing work.
- Report the spread of the output index across organisations, not only the employee-weighted means.

---

## Suggested revisions to the headline claims

| Current claim | Defensible version |
|---|---|
| "Gains in output per hour in every sector… the model is sector-general" | "Manager-reported output stayed near baseline in knowledge-work sectors. It fell in customer-facing sectors, where reversions were concentrated." |
| "Implying an increase in output per scheduled hour of 23.4%" | "Up to 23.4% per scheduled hour. The gain per hour actually worked is unknown because actual hours were not measured." |
| "Sick days fell by 36%" | Report sick days per scheduled day, and use a baseline that matches the season. |
| "Revenue offers no sign that output was sacrificed" | "Nominal revenue rose 1.4%, which is probably a fall in real terms." |

The recommendation for a comparison group in future pilots is the right one. I would add **independent measurement of output** and **logging of actual hours worked**, because without those even a controlled design would leave the main number in doubt.
